analysis.title: Margin Call Risk Is Rising As Liquidity Tightens
key_insights: Liquidity conditions have been tightening for several months, and the author links this to last week's funding squeezes and margin calls in markets.
Record leverage leaves markets exposed because a liquidity shortage makes it harder to refinance debt used to fund asset positions.
The global and US real yield curves have steepened sharply as longer-term real yields rise while short-term rates fall.
Global real M1 growth has been declining, and an energy-driven rise in inflation means more liquidity is needed just to cover higher input costs, leaving less for risk assets.
Net margin debt is about $1.5 trillion, a high in dollar and GDP terms but not in market-cap terms. The cost of carrying it is at an all-time peak versus GDP and exceeds the March 2000 level.

G10 excess liquidity (real M1 growth minus economic growth, 3-month smoothed) is negative. The author says that typically means the market soon sells off and funding rates capitulate, with 2007 the main exception.
Hedge funds owe nearly $4 trillion to prime brokers, with some overlap with the margin debt figure. At SOFR + 50 bps, annual repayments would exceed $150 billion (data to Q2 2026).
Hedge funds added shorts instead of cutting losing core AI longs, then last week gross positions fell sharply as funds started selling some long tech positions.

Gold fell 3.7% on Friday even though yields and the dollar both fell. The author reads this as liquidity-driven selling, and gold's correlation with stocks has risen on down days and fallen on up days.
The Treasury General Account (TGA) rose to its highest level last week as T-bill settlements picked up. Treasury expected it to exceed $1 trillion, and SOFR rose relative to the fed funds rate.

Hedge fund shorting of equity indices such as the Nasdaq, along with less bullish speculative activity in single stocks, is lifting index correlation. The author says this adds widening pressure on credit spreads, which tends to tighten bank loan standards.
The US midterm elections on the report date and speculation about President Trump's actions afterward add event risk. The author sees a higher than normal likelihood of greater price declines.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Historically followed by equity sell-offs and funding rate capitulation.

risk_factors: Margin calls and forced selling if liquidity keeps tightening and collateral values stop rising.
Reflexive loop in which falling liquidity lowers stock prices, and those stocks collateralise the funding behind positions.
Rising funding costs against record leverage at margin investors and hedge funds.
Higher TGA balance tightening short-term funding.
Wider credit spreads leading to tighter bank loan standards and fewer loans made or rolled over.
Election and policy uncertainty around the US midterms.
vol_and_positioning: Hedge funds added short positions, including in equity indices such as the Nasdaq, instead of cutting core AI longs, which lowered net exposure for prime brokers.
Gross hedge fund positions fell sharply last week as funds sold some long tech positions.
Gold's correlation with stocks has risen on down days and fallen on up days.
Rising index correlation is expected to add widening pressure on credit spreads.
geopolitical: US midterm elections held on the report date.
Speculation about what President Trump may do at home and abroad once he no longer has to face the electorate.
